synopsis: The booklet frames collision-mitigation tuning as constrained multi-objective optimization: missed or late interventions are a hard constraint, while false warnings, unnecessary braking and productivity loss are optimized with the Pareto front visible [f136]. The glossary further recommends putting the human-factors rate on one axis of that front [f14442]. Chapter 9 recommends preserving visibility so trade-offs become documented safety-policy decisions rather than hidden weights; evolutionary methods make trade-offs explicit but do not determine which Pareto point is acceptable [f6672, f6971, f6973]. Pareto-front, NSGA-II and other evolutionary methods, referenced to Deb et al. (2002), are described as robust and simple to parallelise over simulation, but they require many evaluations [f6970, f6972].

relations.note: Adds the human-factors rate as a Pareto-front axis to the constrained tuning formulation.
Explains why the Pareto front should remain visible: documented safety-policy trade-offs.
Explicit trade-offs support visible, documented decisions rather than hidden weights.
Selecting an acceptable Pareto point remains a policy decision.
The constrained optimization framework still requires policy selection of an acceptable Pareto point.
Explicit trade-offs justify keeping the Pareto front visible during tuning.
Adds evaluation-cost limitations to the methods' robustness and simulation parallelisability.
